Kuṟuntokai 130. Veḷḷi Vīti(yār): the confidante / SHE
Tolkāppiyam Poruḷatikāram Iḷampūraṇam ed. Citambaram Piḷḷai. 1928

lg.l: [The heroine] standing with duty to the confidante

with speech of an honourable nature without contradiction;In Nakkīrar’s commentary to IA 14, he states that when her companion reveals the relationship to the foster mother, she does so by speaking in such a way that does not contradict the mother’s knowledge, the heroine’s greatness, the heroine’s fidelity, her companion’s chaperoning, the heroine’s modesty, or the ways of the world. The TNV here deviates slightly by starting this situation with the heroine revealing the relationship. Presumably the non-contradiction refers to the same things.
the foster mother praising the [heroine]; the confidante informing [the foster mother];
the female diviner of ancient wisdom saying, ‘[It is] Murukaṉ’;

[the heroine] considering thatI assume atu refers to the incorrect conclusion that the heroine’s lovesickness is caused by Murukaṉ, as this will result in the initiation of the veṟi ritual. and despairing; [the confidante] questioning [the priest] in opposition [to the ritual];
[the confidante] saying, ‘[It is] a lie’; [the heroine] resolving to die;
[the confidante] saying, ‘It is not the custom’; the woman agreeing;

her companion indirectly addressingThis phrase paṭarkkaimuṉ ṉilai is a way to express indirect communication. One could literally translate it as: ‘standing in front [of one person, addressing] a third person’. muṉ ṉilai is the term for the second person, so connotes a direct form of address, and paṭarkkai is the term for the third person. [the foster mother] during the veṟi dance;
the foster mother speaking to the birth mother;

[the birth mother] rejecting the marriage proposal; [the heroine] becoming depressed; [the confidante] clearing [the heroine’s low mood];maiyal and teḷittal go together. First the heroine’s mood literally ‘blackens’ (i.e., she becomes depressed), then her friend ‘clears’ this mental darkness (i.e., she comforts her).
the birth mother telling themThis refers to the heroine’s older male relatives. what was said;

and accepting the young men [of the hero]iḷaiyōr is a designation used for the young men of the family. Here, it is understood to refer to the young men of the hero’s family and/or retinue, which is supported by the commentary based on the final example poem cited. In his commentary to TP 170n and TP 171n, Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar also uses it in this context. This then is the situation where the hero and his people are accepted for marriage. Another option is that it could refer to the heroine’s young male relatives (iḷaiyōr refers to them in TNV 23), in which case this final speech situation would be the elliptical couple ‘being acceptable to the young men [of her family]’. A third option, though not a strong one, is that iḷaiyōr could refer to the young couple, in which case the heroine’s elliptical family would accept their relationship. This has no parallels. – they say [these situations are] the revelation [of the relationship].

div.p: eṉpatu aṟattoṭu nilai yām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which standing with duty occurs.

kaṟpiṉōṭuṅ kāvalōṭunalattiṉōṭuṅ kulattiṉōṭum ulakiṉōṭumāṟukōḷ illā moḻiyāṟ ṟalaimakaḷ tōḻikkaṟattoṭu niṟṟaṉ mutal āka varaivetir kōṭal īṟākac collap paṭṭa vivai yaṟattoṭu nilai yām eṉṟu colluvar pulavar eṉṟa vāṟu.

Beginning with the heroine standing with duty to the confidante with a speech that does not contradict: [her] fidelity, [the confidante’s] watchful protection, [her] goodness, [her] lineage, and [the custom of] the world, and ending with accepting marriage – these that have been mentioned are standing with duty, so the erudite scholars say.

lg.l: O friend, may you live! The other day,

while I was sinking in the deep pond, a man stopped [me]takai-ttal can be understood as ‘to stop’ here, where the hero prevented her drowning and saved her, or one can understand it in another sense – ‘to grab’. In this case he would take hold of her and lift her up. Purely based on expected meaning, the second is preferable, but this is an attested meaning only for the weak root, so may not quite apply. If he ‘bound’ or ‘fastened’ her – the equivalent meanings for the strong root – it would not be as attractive an option. and,
with his great broad hand hanging down, dragged me out.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṭōḻikkaṟattoṭu niṉṟatu.
This is the heroine having stood with duty to the confidante.

lg.l: The innocent girl with the slender waist,
wide eminent hips, large breasts, dark eyes, and a red mouth,

has reallyperitu can either be understood as an adverb or as a predicate. This translation takes it as an adverb. As a predicate: ‘she has become the big (with the sense of ‘important’) thing – the good sweet life…’ become [like]Though it is not expressed in the Tamil, and so is not translated, the idea here is that the foster mother is realising that the heroine is ready for marriage. the one good sweet life
for a most worthy [man] who will obtain her shining goodness.

div.p: eṉpatu cevili talaimakaḷai makaṭkōlañ ceytatu.
This is the foster mother having done the daily adornment of the heroine.

lg.l: Where is he? The man who set offpaṭar tantōṉē can just as well mean ‘the man who gave affliction’. The current translation takes tā-/taru-tal as a modal auxiliary, but it can be taken independently with its full semantic weight. Both interpretations are attested. See Kali 81.23 for ‘bring affliction’ and PN 301.14 for ‘set off’.
after stroking her fragrant forehead saying, ‘Would that I had you’,I am not sure what is expressed by the optative here in peṟuka. I understand it as expressing a wish.
when the dark tresses of the one with the excellent earrings

div.p: eṉpatu cevili talaimakaḷaip puṉaintiyārō vivaḷai eytutaṟkariya peruntakai eṉat tōḻi aṟattoṭu niṉṟatu.

The confidante stands with duty when the foster mother, having decorated the heroine, says, ‘Who is that most worthy man who has the right toThis is a literal translation. What it gets at is that the hero is deserving of the right to come and speak to her – eligible, in other words. approach her?’

lg.l: Don’t grieve with your unknowingeyyā, the negative peyareccam of ey-tal, can be understood two ways. The most common meaning of the root is ‘to reach/attain’. If one were to understand it thus, then it could refer to the heart ‘that has not attained [what it wants]’ – knowledge about the state of the heroine. However, in the context of the poem, the less common, but still attested, meaning ‘to know/understand’ makes better sense. The foster mother’s heart does not know the cause of the heroine’s weakened state. See Kali 124.9, 13 for the verb with this sense. heart! Live on!

There is also the fallingIs paṭṭatu a verbal noun, as translated, or a neuter singular participial noun? And what exactly does it mean? The root paṭu-tal could reasonably mean ‘to fall’ or ‘to happen’ in this case. Taking the first meaning, it refers to the literal falling of the beans as a part of the divination ritual. The second refers to either the result of the divination or the act of divining via the beans – ‘there is the occurrence of/on account of the Molucca beans’. If one takes it to mean ‘fall’, then the form ought to be a verbal noun, as there is an oblique relationship to the Molucca beans, meaning they cannot be ‘the thing that fell’. If we take it as ‘to happen’, then either analysis of the form makes sense, and results in essentially the same meaning. of the faultless Molucca beans.
That itself is, from their faultless sight, the clarity

[of her] becoming a divine celestial form whose shining life is confused.Is the idea that she is turning into a divine form as a result of Murukaṉ’s possession, or is his divine form appearing? I feel the former is more likely due to the preceding relative construction, which only really makes sense if the girl is the subject – it is not Murukaṉ’s life that is confused.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ vēṟupāṭu kaṇṭu cevili viṉavak kaṭṭuvicci colliyatu.
This is the female diviner having spoken when, after seeing the changes in the heroine, the foster mother questions [their cause].

lg.l: Mother is ignorant. [The vēlaṉ] dances the veṟi ritual.
O heart, what will become of

our conduct worthy of our faultless family, our modestyAs mentioned before, the semantic field of nāṇ encompasses shame and modesty. When applied to a young girl, it often has positive connotations as it shows that you understand how to function in society. In some cases translating it as ‘shame’, even though that is its base meaning, can be misleading.

and our fidelitykaṟpu is difficult to translate. As mentioned previously, it refers to the married stage of life in poetic theory. Within poetry, it can either refer to that stage, or to the behaviour suitable to the stage. One also commonly finds it translated as ‘chastity’, though that carries puritanical connotations that are not always present in the poetry. worthy of goodnessnalam is an equally loaded term. In some cases it can have a sexual undertone. It is translated literally here, but another common translation is ‘virtue’. in [this] house?

div.p: eṉpatu cevili veṟi kālkoḷḷat talaimakaḷ iraṅkiyatu.
This is the heroine having wept when the foster mother initiated the veṟi dance.

lg.l: After examining tiṟa ṉāṭi could be split differently as tiṟaṉ āṭi. The first line could then be a reference to the completion of the veṟi dance, which might then be the ‘undying custom’. This would, however, require a subject-changing viṉaiyeccam. the one way of undying custom,Presumably this custom is the practice of aṟattoṭu nilai – the revelation of the heroine’s affair to the mother.
what if we told [mother] over there,I am not sure how to take ā vayiṉ. This translation simply takes it literally. O friend?
the hot pain of love has gone beyond [your control].

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ āṟṟāmai yuṇarnta tōḻi yaṟattoṭu niṟṟaṟakkateṉṟatu.
This is the confidante, who had realised that the heroine was unable to bear [the situation], having said, ‘It is appropriate to stand with duty.’

lg.l: What is the point of any of that?The standard translation for ākuvatu uṇṭō is ‘what is the benefit?’ See Kuṟaḷ 315.
Just like that, O woman with a waist slender like the vañci tree,
while your heart looked on, he lied.

div.p: eṉpatu āṟṟāḷ āy niṉṟa talaimakaḷait tōḻi poym moḻintaṉaṉ eṉa vāṟṟuvittatu.
This is the confidante having comforted the heroine, who was standing [there] unable to bear [the ritual], by saying, ‘He is telling lies.’

lg.l: Because, after tellinguṇartti, taken here as an absolutive, is homophonous with the second person subjunctive. If one took it that way, then the heroine would be telling the confidante to go tell mother, as she will not be doing so herself on account of having to continue living with her. mother in keeping with this custom,
we are of a lasting life on this earth,

I, with a body like gold and shining ornaments,The final line can also be understood as an address: ‘I will leave… O one with the body like gold and shining jewels’. Because of the placement of the pronoun immediately after, it made for a more natural syntactic structure to read it as a description of the heroine.
will release this sweet life now without informing her.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ aṟattoṭu nilai maṟuttatu.
This is the heroine having refused to stand with duty.

lg.l: It is not love; it is not fidelity;
and it is not conduct that came with goodnessnaṉṟu here carries connotations of virtue, I think. –

the issueThe ‘issue’ is the heroine’s desire to die instead of revealing the truth from the last poem. of which the women with beautiful banglesInstead of referring to the heroine, this might refer to women in general. The last two lines of the poem would then have to be construed differently. The issues about which the women speak (or the manner in which they speak) would be the object of āṟṟu-tal. The point of the poem would be that the confidante is telling the heroine that she will only be acting virtuously once she has revealed herself and become their topic of discussion. spoke –
unless [you] desire to bear it.In other words, the confidante is saying that the only path to a virtuous life is for the heroine to keep living and expose the secret.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi yaṟattoṭu nilai nayappikkak kūṟiyatu.
This is the confidante having talked [to the heroine] to persuade her to stand with duty.

lg.l: I cannot bear it, O friend,

unless I tooPresumably, the -um particle in yāṉum is an eccavummai and the hero is the other element in the co-ordination – she will only feel happy once she has felt the same cool wind that he felt. Is it then an oblique way to say that she longs to be with him and where he is, i.e., be married, and this necessitates ‘standing with duty’? feel the wind after it stirred
inside the grove where flowers hang on his mountain.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ aṟattoṭu nilai nayantatu.
This is the heroine having longed to stand with duty.

lg.l: If you intend to ease the pain
of the girl with the cool grace and giveeṇṇiṉai koṭutti: See KT 362.5 for the exact same morpho-syntactic construction where it functions as a muṟṟeccam. an offering,

would the chest of the lord still eat it?The offering will be given to Murukaṉ, the supposed cause of the heroine’s troubles, and by asking this question, the confidante is making clear that one would have to give an offering to the hero for her problems to abate.

div.p: eṉpatu veṟi yāṭṭiṉ kaṇ vēlaṉ mēl vaittut tōḻi yaṟattoṭu niṉṟatu.
This is the confidante having stood with duty after putting [it] on the priest at the veṟi ritual.

lg.l: [You are] foolish, may you live, O Murukaṉ,

by comingvarutalāṉ can also be a locative, rather than an instrumental as translated here. In which case: ‘foolish… when coming…’ In practice, this amounts to much the same thing. to appease the woman’s suffering,

having declared, ‘He is a total stranger.’This refers to the hero. Murukaṉ is a fool because he is lying about the fact that the hero is the cause of the heroine’s misery. One could also take this as a first person. In that case, Murukaṉ would be foolish for coming just to say that he is not the cause. The source poems (see apparatus) suggest the former interpretation.

div.p: eṉpatu murukaṉ mēl vaittaṟattoṭu niṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having stood with duty after putting [it] on Murukaṉ.

lg.l: In [her] youth, when the sprouting teeth were not yet full,

she gladly boreEither in the sense that she wore it and/or carried it around with her, or that she bore the metaphorical burden of this gesture lightly when she was young and now realises what it meant. the chaplet with open outer petals
that the bright shining man offered.

div.p: eṉpatu cevili viṉavat tōḻi yaṟattoṭu niṉṟatu.
This is the confidante having stood with duty when the foster mother questioned [her].

lg.l: The girl with the garland of glowing clusters does not forget the lord,
who embraced and lifted us out as we were sinking

in a verykayam cāl is literally: ‘to be abundant with depth’. deepI do not think one can take kayam in its most common meaning of a ‘tank’ or ‘pond’. The confidante and heroine were caught in the currents, so were clearly not in a still body of water. ‘Depth’ is a post-Caṅkam meaning and makes more sense here (see Periya Tirumoḻi 8.5.4.1 for an attestation). whirling current.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: She has grown wise to it!mutukkuṟaintaṉaḷ has two opposite meanings. This translation comes from an entry in the TL from the compound verb mutukkuṟai-tal. A derived form, mutukkuṟaivu, is also present and is defined as either ‘great wisdom’, ‘the pubescence of girls’, or ‘innocence’. The ideas of innocence or foolishness are suggested by the etymology: mutumai (‘great knowledge’) + kuṟai-tal (‘to lack’). Were this to be the intended meaning, the poem would bemoan the fact that the heroine is not yet ready for this relationship, or that this has been going on for a long time, since she was young, which shows it is serious. The other interpretation – that the heroine has grown wise – has been chosen as it has more textual parallels (cf. NA 366, Kuṟaḷ 707). She has grown wise to it!
The girl whose breasts have still not come has grown wise
to the chaplet and bright spear of the man from the mountains.

div.p: eṉpatu cevili naṟṟāykkaṟattoṭu niṉṟatu.
This is the foster mother having stood with duty to the birth mother.

lg.l: O, but she is so young! Seeing the whole clan
is [like] seeing the sea packed with conches and violent waves.
Clearly understanding the bird omens, the nakṣatra,
and other things is the duty of the elders.

div.p: eṉpatu varaivu maṟuttatu.
This is [the birth mother] having rejected the marriage [proposal].

lg.l: Of course she is feeling downiḷi varu cintaiyaḷ could also mean: ‘she is one whose thoughts come with scorn’, if we take the TL definition for iḷi, ‘scorn’. In this translation, it is understood as a root noun from iḷital that, in its intransitive meaning, carries more of the weight of sadness, though of course this sadness could be caused by disgrace or scorn.

because of the considerate oneIn practice, I have taken aruḷiṉāṉ as an ākupeyar, referring to the gracious hero. One can also understand aṇi tikaḻ neñciṉ as an aṉmoḻittokai (‘exocentric compound’ or bahuvrīhi compound; ‘the one with consideration in his beautiful shining heart’), in which case aruḷiṉāṉ would not be a metonymy. With a variant reading, one could also analyse it as a participial derivation. For more on that, see the critical notes in the apparatus. with a beautiful shining heart,Or, ‘the man with consideration/grace in [his] beautiful shining heart’, or, ‘the consideration/grace of the man with a beautiful shining heart’.
who gave us the great leaf skirt that shines with brightness.

div.p: eṉpatu varaivu maṟutta vaḻit talaimakaḷ āṟṟāḷ āyiṟṟu.
This is the heroine having become unable to bear it when [the birth mother] rejected the marriage [proposal].

lg.l: You have suffered. Live, my friend!

Surelymātō here seems to have a more assertive quality, rather than its normal rhetorical function. Perhaps by this post-Caṅkam stage of the language, this was more common, especially when affixed to a perfective verb. This kind of construction is rare in the Caṅkam corpus – only four occurrences were found. In this text alone, there are five. our relatives long for
the lord with the long perfect leaf-tip spear,

div.p: eṉpatu varaivuṇarnta tōḻi talaimakaḷai yāṟṟuvittatu.
This is the confidante, who was aware of the marriage [situation], having comforted the heroine.

lg.l: After considering the conduct befitting [our]Whose family’s conduct? This can either refer to the hero and his family acting in an appropriate way towards the heroine’s family, in which case their marriage proposal deserves to be accepted, or to the heroine’s family looking at what would be the appropriate way for them to act, and deciding to accept the proposal. There is not a huge difference in the meaning of the poem. This translation takes the second option, as it does not require a subject-changing viṉaiyeccam. family,
the [correct] conclusion is to bestow the chaste girl

with young breasts carrying ornaments to the lord worthy of goodness.As I understand it, the idea here is that the lord is worthy of taking on her goodness, which may be a euphemism for marriage or virginity. Another way to translate would be to take cāl-tal as ‘to abound in/be full of’, in which case the lord would be full of nalam. This is normally a quality associated with women, so that seems less likely, unless it is another euphemistic way to express his suitability for marriage, which is the point of the mother’s speech.

div.p: eṉpatu naṟṟāy tamarkkaṟattoṭu niṉṟatu.
This is the birth mother having stood with duty to the relatives.

lg.l: Considering the customs of [our]As above, this could also refer to the heroine’s family observing the customs of the hero’s family and deciding they are worthy. In that case, one could take the -um in marapum as distributive and read varavu nōkki instead of varavum nōkki, so there would no longer be any co-ordination. This would translate to: ‘Considering your approach along this way, you worthy people with customs from an ancient sky-touching lineage…’ ancient sky-touching lineage,
and your approach, you worthy people, along this way, we have accepted.
Otherwise, even if we were to obtain all these three worlds,

div.p: eṉpatu varaivetir koṇṭatu. 22.
This is [the heroine’s family] having accepted the marriage [proposal].

standOff.note: Cf. TP203.1–2: aṟattoṭu niṟkuṅ kālat taṉṟi | yaṟattiyaṉ marapila ṭōḻi yeṉpa ||
Cf. IA29.6: aṟattoṭu niṟṟa ṟōḻikku murittē ||
Cf. TP139i: veḷippaṭai tāṉē kaṟpiṉo ṭoppiṉu | ñāṅkark kiḷanta mūṉṟu poruḷāka | varaiyātu pirital kiḻavoṟ killai ||
Cf. IA26: veḷippaṭai tāṉē virikkuṅ kālait | tantai tāyē taṉṉaiya reṉṟāṅ | kaṉṉava raṟiyap paṇpā kummē ||

Though it is uncommon to find a speech situation that comprises only two verbal nouns (poṉṟutal tuṇital, in this case), one can still make sense of it. I am not convinced that UVC’s correction here improves the text meaningfully. I have not been able to find any parallels that support his reading. Later in this text, in TNV 24, poem 4, one finds varal tuṇinta (‘resolved to come / on coming’). This is admittedly not from a cūttiram, which employs a slightly different idiom from the poems, but it does show that this author used the formula ‘verbal noun + tuṇi-tal’ to express a similar meaning to what we expect here. All in all, I do not think there is sufficient evidence to deviate from C1.
UVC’s emendation makes sense here. It would be highly unlikely for eṉ-tal to follow eṉ-tal as in C1. UVC’s solution is the most minimal sensible intervention.

Both the strong form (C2, Cām) and the weak (C1) make some sense here. This edition deviates from the C1 reading on the strength of the commentarial interpretation that this act of ‘clearing’ the heroine’s mood is a transitive action performed by the confidante.

Again, both readings, iḷaiyōrkku and iḷaiyōṟku, make sense in the context. For a discussion on the possible interpretations of the chosen reading, see the footnotes to the translation. UVC’s emendation necessitates understanding the final situation slightly differently, with the heroine’s family accepting the young man, in this case the hero. In the absence of convincing parallels to support this reading, this edition follows C1.

Cf. IAC14, p. 126: eṟṟiṉoṭu māṟukoḷḷāmaiyōveṉiṉ, tāyaṟiviṉoṭu māṟukoḷḷāmaiyun, talaimakaḷperumaiyoṭu māṟukoḷḷāmaiyun, talaimakaḷatu kaṟpiṉoṭu māṟukoḷḷāmaiyun, tōḻitaṉatu kāvaloṭu māṟukoḷḷāmaiyum, nāṇiṉoṭu māṟukoḷḷāmaiyum, ulakiṉoṭu māṟukoḷḷāmaiyumeṉakoḷka.
Cf. AV48.1: talaivi pāṅkik kaṟattoṭu niṟkum
Cf. IAC14, p. 127–128: emmaikkūḻaikkaṟṟaik kuḻavippirāyattu māḻaikalanta ēḻainīrmaiyāroṭu nāṭkōlañceytu viḷaiyāṭivammiṉeṉṟu pōkkiṉāy

The two editions both print nāṭkōlañ, which is what one finds in the IAC. As this refers to a daily adornment of a daughter by a mother figure, C1 makes just as good sense. It makes explicit that this is an act performed on/for the daughter. It is reasonable to assume that there were multiple ways to describe this custom and that over time they became standardised into nāṭkōlam.
Cf. AV53.1–2: cevili | pāṅkiyai viṉavum
Cf. AV178.1: miṉṉiṭai vēṟṟumai kaṇṭutāy viṉāvuḻi

Cf. IAC14, p. 126–127: teyvattai vaṇaṅkak kaṟpaḻiyumeṉṟu talaimakaḷ āṟṟāḷām. allatūum oḻukkakkuṟṟak kuṟaipāṭu nīṅki ōṅkivarāniṉṟa tolkulam maṇikkalaṅ katuvāyppaṭṭatupola yāṉ tōṉṟi ivvakai aṇaṅkāṭṭu aṟiyātu aṇaṅkāṭṭu eṭuttukkoḷḷappaṭṭeṉavum
As in other places, the IAC just mentions this speech situation in its prose section without quoting a poem for it. The relevant section is provided.

The C1 reading makes little sense and it is almost certainly corrupt. The one way to possibly understand it is by taking veṭṭiṉ as an oblique noun meaning ‘cutting’. At a stretch, this could refer to some feature of the veṟi dance where the vēlaṉ (lit.: ‘man with the spear’) brandishes his weapon. There is no evidence that this is a part of the veṟi ritual and it also distorts the normal nuance of veṭṭu-tal, which is really ‘to cut off’. Accepting the need for emendation, I think UVC’s proposal is perfectly reasonable. It makes good sense and is as invasive as the other obvious option – veṟiyiṉkaṇ.
Cf. AV53.2–3: cevili | pāṅkiyai viṉavum
Cf. AV48.2: pāṅki cevilik kaṟattoṭu niṟkum
Cf. IAC14, p. 128: iḵtu aṟivatu aṟiyākkālattu nikaḻntataṉai aṟivataṟintu
Cf. TK294.1–2: iḷaiyā ḷivaḷaiyeṉ collip paravutu mīreyiṟu | muḷaiyā vaḷaviṉ mutukkuṟaintāḷ

IAC29, p. 184–185: eṉṟaviṭattu iḵteṉakkup paṭṭatu, iṉṉaviṭattu oru ñāṉṟu nīyum āyaṅkaḷun taḻaiyuṅ kaṇṇiyuṅkōṭaṟku eṉṉic ciṟitu nīṅkiṉāy; yāṉ niṉṟu oru maṇiccuṉai kaṇṭēṉ; kaṇṭa ammaṇiccuṉaitāṉ āmpalē kuvaḷaiyē neytalē tāmaraiyē eṉṟippūkkaḷāl mayaṅki mētakkatu kaṇṭu vēṭkaiyāṉ aṭuvāṉ iḻintēṉ; iḻukkik kuṭṭam pukkēṉ; pukkut tōḻiyōveṉa, nī aṅṅaṉaṅ kēḷāyāyiṉāyāka, oru tōṉṟal tōṉṟi vantu eṉatu tuyarnīkkutaṟkākat taṉ kai nīṭṭiṉāṉ. nīṭṭiṉaviṭattu malakkattāṉ niṉkaiyeṉap paṟṟiṉēṉ; paṟṟa, vāṅkik karaimēṉiṟīi nīṅkiṉāṉ

The PK poems are spoken by the confidante to the foster mother, whereas the cited IAC prose passage details the same situation of the hero rescuing the heroine from the flood, but it is spoken by the heroine to the confidante, as in the TNV poem.

I do not understand the rationale behind UVC’s deviation from C1. Perhaps this was just a simple error? māṇkuḻai makes better sense and it is a more common collocation in the corpus. In the fourth example poem to TNV 16, the poet also uses this phrase to describe the heroine.

iṉaiyal vāḻi is a phrase used in other places by this poet (see \hyperref[ed-TNV15-poem3]{TNV 15, poem 3} and \hyperref[ed-TNV15-poem5]{poem 5}). In addition, one finds a similar phrase in Kali 27.22 – nōy mali neñcamōṭu iṉaiyal. The C1 and C2 reading is also difficult to make sense of.

Some emendation here is necessary. I could not make sense of the C1 reading, which was printed by UVC. For teyva vāṇuru to make any sense, one would have to accept vāṇ as an alternate form of vāḷ (‘bright’), or that there has been some uncommon sandhi. There is no evidence of vāṇ’s existence, nor of a sandhi of prevocalic ḷ → ṇ. Such a change only occurs when it precedes a nasal, and there is no way to make sense of this phrase by dissolving the sandhi with a nasal (vāḷ nuru?). The orthographic similarity between ṇ and ṉ suggests a scribal error may have introduced this corruption. What UVC understood from the phrase he printed, I cannot guess. In further support of this edition’s emendation is the KKms reading. It is clearly corrupted but it reads -ṉuru. Perhaps within the corrupted text, traces of the original remained.
Cf. AiN242.1–3: aṟiyā maiyiṉ veṟiyeṉa mayaṅki | yaṉṉaiyu maruntuya ruḻantaṉa ḷataṉā | leyyātu viṭutalō koṭitē

I suspect UVC may have emended here due to the koḷu. veṟi kālkoḷḷa (‘when [the foster mother] initiates the veṟi’) is basically synonymous to UVC’s proposed reading veṟimuṟai nuṭaṅku (‘the veṟi dance begins’). The C1 reading nuṭaṅkum is, however, a perfectly natural verb for the ritual, meaning ‘to sway’ and by extension ‘to dance’. It is not a consistent feature of the TNV that the koḷu-s mirror the language of the poems, so I do not see strong grounds for emendation.

The poem does not make sense with C1’s reading aṟivāḷ as this would be a positive pronominal derivation, where the expected form would be a negative. The whole point is that the heroine’s mother does not know the reality of the situation, as one finds in the AiN example quoted. If one were to read aṟivāḷ, then the heroine might be lamenting the fact that her mother will come to know about her relationship through the ritual, but that is not the established trope.

Presumably a scribe simply confused the orthographically similar va and la at some point to produce the C1 reading. One can make some sense of it – the final line would translate to: ‘[our] fidelity worthy of goodness in [our] house.’ illuḻi, however, is not a collocation I found anywhere else and it is a less natural reading than the common ivvuḻi.
C1 incorrectly applies sandhi here. This is an occasional feature of the manuscript. See TNV 17, poem 8, for example.
Cf. AN52.12–15: yākkai | yiṉṉuyir kaḻiva tāyiṉu niṉmaka | ḷāyamala ruṇkaṭ pacalai | kāma nōyeṉac ceppā tīmē ||

This is a marginal call. One can make good sense of both immuṟai and immaṟai. UVC’s emendation is possibly a bit smoother: ‘You shall tell mother this secret’. I am inclined to accept the still sensible lectio difficilior reported in C1.

Cf. NA236.3–10: oyyeṉac ciṟitāṅ kuyiriyar paiyeṉa | muṉṟiṟ koḷiṉē nantuvaḷ periteṉa | niraiya neñcat taṉṉaik kuyttāṇ | ṭuraiyiṉi vāḻi tōḻi puraiyi | ṉuṇṇē relvaḷai ñekiḻttōṉ kuṉṟat | taṇṇa ṉeṭuvarai yāṭit taṇṇeṉa | viyalaṟai mūḻkiya vaḷiyeṉ | pacalai yākan tīṇṭiya ciṟitē ||

For this reading, tuḻaiik, to make sense, one needs to understand it as a subject-changing viṉaiyeccam. UVC’s emendation removes this need, and a peyareccam does indeed read more fluently, but it is unnecessary.

UVC’s emendation (cintaiyaṉ) could be interpreted two ways – either as a first person or third person masculine pronominalised noun. In both cases, one can understand the poem without significantly changing its meaning, but just the speaker. My assumption is that UVC understood it as a first person form, in which case the poem reads as a personal lamentation. The first line: ‘Of course I have low-spirited thoughts!’ Possibly he thought this reading aligned more neatly with the koḷu, which emphasises the heroine’s desolation. This does not, however, mean that the heroine has to be the speaker. The TNV koḷu-s do not consistently name speaker and addressee. I would also argue against this interpretation based on the poem itself. The final cīr of the first line suggests this is spoken by the confidante. Unfortunately, I do not have corpus-wide statistics on this, but my impression is that the confidante is more likely to speak on behalf of the heroine than the other way around. The first person plural pronoun nam suggests that this is the case, so I do not find this rationale for emendation convincing. The other way of taking cintaiyaṉ, as a masculine, requires an abstruse interpretation, or the hero’s sadness to be the focus of the poem. In the first case, iḷi varu cintaiyaṉ would refer to the hero who is ‘one of whom thoughts come [with] low spirits’, i.e., thinking about him makes the heroine sad. The second would have to be understood as the heroine losing her ability to bear the pain of the hero and saying: ‘Of course he is feeling down! He is a considerate man…’ This is not necessarily what one would expect in such a poem. Additionally, there is no reason why the poet should have used two different pronominal endings to refer to the same person in the same poem, namely cintaiyaṉ and aruḷiṉāṉ. Without any manuscript evidence supporting the emendation, I see no reason not to maintain the more straightforward and understandable C1 reading.

My feeling is that UVC emended here with etukai in mind. As discussed elsewhere (see \S\ref{sec:ornamentation}), this is not a consistent feature of these poems, so I do not think it is sufficient reason to emend. To be fair, there is a comparatively high incidence of etukai in the poems preceding and following this one, but there is no reason why that would not be coincidental. One could also argue that aḷi tikaḻ (‘compassionate and shining’, ‘shining with compassion’) might be considered the lectio difficilior, but not by a significant margin, so I do not see a good enough reason to emend.
